phase_audit.historical_basis: France and Germany signed an economic partnership agreement concerning Morocco in February 1909.
French forces intervened at Fez in April-May 1911 amid revolt and pressure on the sultan.
Spain, believing French action implicated German-French coordination and acting without consulting France, occupied Larache and its hinterland in early June 1911.
German diplomacy interpreted French and Spanish moves as coordinated partition and sent the gunboat Panther to Agadir on 1 July 1911.
Britain publicly signaled its position during the crisis in Lloyd George's Mansion House speech on 21 July 1911, widely interpreted as a warning to Germany.
phase_audit.source: Keith Wilson, The Agadir Crisis, the Mansion House Speech, and the Double-Edgedness of Agreements, The Historical Journal 15(3), DOI 10.1017/S0018246X00002806

phase_audit.historical_basis: Franco-German negotiations proceeded while Spain sought involvement but was excluded from the Berlin discussion.
The crisis was resolved by the 4 November 1911 Franco-German agreement; Germany recognized France's special position in Morocco while receiving territorial concessions in French Equatorial Africa.
phase_audit.source: U.S. Office of the Historian historical documents; Jean-Marc Delaunay, Moroccan Crises 1905-1911
